claim.subject: Personal & Social Development
claim.name: Social roles and changing responsibilities
claim.description: Describe familiar social roles and relationships, connect them with responsibilities toward other people and the environment, and explain how a setting, event or changing circumstances can alter a role, relationship or duty. Use everyday examples without assuming a particular family structure or requiring private personal disclosure.
evidence: Describe a familiar role, such as pupil, friend, family member or someone helping care for a plant or shared place, and explain a responsibility that comes with it.
Compare one person’s roles, relationships and responsibilities in two settings, explaining why a duty or way of relating to others differs.

Explain how a provided event or change in circumstances alters a responsibility or relationship, including a care duty toward the environment; naming an event or expressing a feeling alone is insufficient.
Apply the role–duty–circumstance relationship to a new supplied scenario, without treating duties as fixed by gender or a single family arrangement.
claim.assessmentPrompt: In a supplied story, the same child, Ari, is a pupil at school and helps care for a garden. Ari knows the school well; a new pupil does not. The story explains that plants need water when soil is dry, and the soil has become dry. Can {{name}} explain how Ari’s roles, relationships and responsibilities differ between the settings, and why each changed circumstance might change a responsibility? They may also use a non-sensitive everyday role of their own.

claimCuration.rationale: The missing operation links familiar social relationships and roles to duties, and explains why circumstances change them. Existing self-description, project-function, family-relationship, coping and rights claims do not test this relationship. This is shared social reasoning, not a country, grade, example or difficulty clone.

closestCandidates.mismatch: Self/background and important people, not role-to-duty or changed-duty explanation.
Functions in collaborative work, not familiar social relationships and changing responsibilities.
Rights/respect reciprocity, not explaining setting/event-dependent roles and duties.
Emotional adjustment and coping, not responsibility reasoning.
Family membership/relationships and origins, not duties or why they change.
Reflecting on friendship/team behaviour, not the general role–duty–circumstance relation.
Preparing for and coping with transitions, not explaining duties.
Language register changes for interpersonal roles, not the social responsibilities themselves.

claimCuration.positiveEvidence: Explains a duty from a role in two settings, including a care duty for a plant/place, and why a stated change changes that duty or relationship.
claimCuration.nearMiss: Only lists people/jobs, project roles or feelings; assigns an identical duty regardless of the setting or change.
claimCuration.transferEvidence: Explains role/duty changes in an unfamiliar supplied school or community-care scenario.
claimCuration.consumerBoundary: New independent claim starts without inferred mastery from any candidate. No existing learner estimate or observation is moved, averaged or reset; repository curation authorizes no private-state change.
claimCuration.prerequisites: No new hard or soft edges: a demonstrated learning need has not been established.
claimCuration.performanceConditions: Fictional scenarios use the same person in both settings and supply environmental facts. The separate source-fit self-application protocol accounts for A1.2/A3.1 using non-sensitive authentic roles/events; no learner study or stored child record is required.

assessmentProtocols.purpose: Account for the authentic self-application condition in the authoring design, without collecting learner records or claiming any learner passed.
assessmentProtocols.materials: Optional blank role/duty card and a simple before/after diagram. The learner can choose ordinary, non-sensitive school roles and a school/class transition; no private family event is required.
instructions: Ask the learner to choose two real everyday roles they have, such as pupil and classmate or classroom helper, and identify the people or place involved.
For each role, ask what responsibility comes with it and why that duty follows from the relationship or setting.
Ask them to choose a non-sensitive real event, such as starting school or joining a new class/activity, and describe a role, relationship or duty before and after it.
Ask why the event changed the responsibility or relationship. A supplied familiar school fact may support recall, but do not supply the causal answer.
Use the separate fictional transfer scenario to check that the reasoning extends beyond a rehearsed autobiography.
assessmentProtocols.evidenceArtifact: A spoken explanation, drawing or short role/duty and before/after representation is sufficient; storage of personal information is not required.

rubric.full: Names authentic everyday roles, connects duties with the related people/place, and explains a genuine role/relationship/responsibility change caused by the chosen event.
rubric.nearMiss: Names a role or event but gives no duty or causal change; only describes a feeling; or succeeds solely with a fictional example.
rubric.transfer: Explains the role/duty/circumstance relationship in the separate unfamiliar supplied school/garden story.

assessmentProtocols.coverageBoundary: This is a source-fit assessment protocol, not a learner-performance study. Full authoring coverage means the required self-application is explicitly accounted for; it does not certify any learner.

assessmentProtocols.materials: Use the three attributed factual case summaries in this dossier, with the brief historical context, read aloud or presented as text. Images, programme enrolment and target-language pronunciation are not required.
assessmentProtocols.historicalContext: Colonial policies in Canada, including residential schooling, separated many Indigenous children from family life and suppressed languages and cultural practices. Indigenous peoples continued their cultures and today lead many forms of renewal. The general history does not establish that every individual or every named project has an identical local history.
instructions: Introduce the historical context in plain, non-graphic language. Do not ask for a learner’s or family’s residential-school testimony.
Attribute each case to its named people/community and source. Distinguish a First Nation, Métis and Inuit case rather than treating one as all Indigenous peoples.
Ask who leads the project, what is being renewed and how that can connect people with family/community knowledge and identity.
Use a second case as a transfer check. Ask which similarities describe the broad relationship and which specific people, language or practices remain different.
Check that the explanation includes the historical disruption and contemporary community agency, not only generic respect or naming peoples.

rubric.full: Explains the historical disruption in introductory terms, identifies community-led action from an attributed case and connects renewal with identity/belonging; transfers the relationship without generalizing one case to all peoples.
rubric.nearMiss: Only names Indigenous peoples, says everyone should be respected, treats cultures as gone or people as only historical, or describes a programme without the history/identity relationship.
rubric.transfer: Explains the corresponding relationship for a second case while retaining its different people, source and practice.

assessmentProtocols.coverageBoundary: Authoring source-fit protocol, not evidence that a learner passed. It teaches about cultural/language renewal, not French or Indigenous-language proficiency. Community programmes are examples of agency, not guaranteed therapeutic outcomes.

assessmentProtocols.materials: Adult prepares a dated, attributed packet for the learner’s actual school using publicly available, locally verified location/resources and appropriate Nation/community territorial and treaty resources, with school/board or municipal statements separately attributed. Supply readable extracts/paraphrases and a legend/key; no private child or home address is needed.
preparationChecks: Verify the public school location and the relevant region, not simply a school name shared with another place.

Consult relevant Indigenous Nation/community resources, applicable treaty accounts and appropriate school/board references. Preserve multiple supported peoples/accounts and identify disagreement or uncertainty instead of deciding exclusive ownership.
Identify whether the packet establishes a treaty, the full name/number and regional/date context. Never invent a numbered treaty or equate every treaty with a sale or extinguishment.
Distinguish any marked current reserve from traditional territory and treaty references. Maps are regional educational resources, not legal parcel determinations.

If suitable local information is missing or conflicting, the local application remains unverified until the adult resolves the resource question; another school’s worked example does not certify this school.
instructions: Introduce traditional territory, treaty reference and reserve as different kinds of information, using the attributed packet and supplied map legend.
Ask the learner to identify the supported traditional territory or territories and applicable treaty for their own school, explaining which source supports each statement.
Ask whether the nearest reserve or the municipal boundary alone would justify the answer and why not.
Use the second worked public-school packet for transfer. Ask what differs, what each source establishes and what cannot be concluded.

rubric.full: Identifies the supported traditional territory or territories and applicable treaty reference for the actual school from the verified packet, keeps accounts attributed, distinguishes a reserve from the broader references, and transfers the distinction to another region without unsupported exclusivity.
rubric.nearMiss: Only names generic Indigenous peoples, copies the first school’s treaty into the second, selects the nearest reserve, collapses every map boundary into territory, or claims the resources establish exclusive parcel title.
rubric.transfer: Uses another region’s packet to identify its supported peoples and treaty reference, retaining its different name/number/date context and resource limits.

assessmentProtocols.coverageBoundary: A source-fit authoring protocol, not a learner pass record. Worked cases demonstrate the design; own-school application requires the adult-prepared locally verified packet. No ceremony participation, private address collection or legal adjudication is required.

assessmentProtocols.materials: Two introductory school scenarios about the same fictional person: a new pupil receives practical patient help, later successfully helps another pupil. Supply concrete events and actions, not a prewritten conclusion about identity.
assessmentProtocols.task: Identify effects of actions on both people, distinguish an immediate feeling from what the person now thinks they can do or what kind of person they are, and explain how the changed relationship/duty and interaction contributed. Compare an unkind response and a constructive alternative without suggesting one event permanently determines identity.
assessmentProtocols.positive: Connect interaction and consequences to a supported self-description/quality or sense of capability, and explain role/duty change across situations.
assessmentProtocols.nearMiss: Says only happy/sad, names a quality without event evidence, or assumes every person reacts identically.
assessmentProtocols.coverageBoundary: Source-fit authoring design, not a learner pass record. Whole contributing claims remain unchanged; no private learner records, mastery transfer or classroom study is required.

assessmentProtocols.materials: Learner chooses non-sensitive examples from ordinary school/community life: a helpful person, familiar place and object/living thing. A class-library book or classroom plant is suitable; no private family possession/photo/address needed.
assessmentProtocols.task: Name the examples and describe the role/purpose of each in the learner’s life, not only its appearance or a favourite label.
assessmentProtocols.positive: Identifies significance and purpose/role across people, places and things in familiar life.
assessmentProtocols.nearMiss: Lists names only or describes object colour with no role/purpose.
assessmentProtocols.coverageBoundary: Source-fit authoring design, not a learner pass record. Whole contributing claims remain unchanged; no private learner records, mastery transfer or classroom study is required.

assessmentProtocols.materials: Shared classroom materials/turn-taking scenario and school garden/place-care scenario. Supply factual care needs (e.g. plants need water when soil is dry); do not make independent plant science an accidental gate.
assessmentProtocols.task: Choose and carry out or demonstrate an appropriate respectful response in each scenario and explain why it matters to people and shared environments. Identify the responsibilities of people in the setting and a constructive alternative to harm.
assessmentProtocols.positive: Understands importance and demonstrates respectful treatment across both people and place, rather than only reciting a rule.
assessmentProtocols.nearMiss: Is kind to people but treats places as irrelevant, or names a rule without explaining its significance.
assessmentProtocols.coverageBoundary: Source-fit authoring design, not a learner pass record. Whole contributing claims remain unchanged; no private learner records, mastery transfer or classroom study is required.

sourceCases.userResponsibility: Adult sets appropriate bins out on the scheduled collection day with accessible space and lids closed; child explains with a model rather than handles real waste or stands near collection trucks.

sourceCases.provider: Toronto Public Library, a City service agency governed by its library board; no need primary learner to memorize appointment/funding law.
sourceCases.userResponsibility: Return borrowed ordinary books using the stated loan period/location rules so others can use them; no actual account or library card action required.
sourceCases.currentLimit: Do not infer universal fixed loan periods for allmaterials or pretend every item can go to anybranch; source has exceptions.

assessmentProtocols.task: Identify the service, government/community provider from the factual card and what it does, then describe a corresponding user role/responsibility and explain why it helps the service work for the community. Transfer to another verified service. Contrast paying/working at an unrelated private shop so merely naming a job is not accepted as the government/community provider relationship.
assessmentProtocols.positive: Correct provider/service relationship and matching user duty with explanation, on two current attributed cases.
assessmentProtocols.nearMiss: Says everyone helps without naming who supplies the service, swaps provider/user duties, or assumes every waste stream has the same operator.
assessmentProtocols.transfer: Another verified local service, retaining its own organizational form and duties.
assessmentProtocols.coverageBoundary: Source-fit authoring design, not a learner pass record. Whole contributing claims remain unchanged; no private learner records, mastery transfer or classroom study is required.

assessmentProtocols.materials: An adult-verified familiar local/school map with two or more distinguishable areas and a few accurate observations or photographs of their characteristics. School areas are an explicit source illustration; no child address or complete town zoning dataset is required.
assessmentProtocols.task: Identify the distinct areas on the map and describe characteristics that distinguish them, such as a wooded park with paths and plants versus a school classroom wing with rooms joined by a hallway. Locate the areas relative to each other and explain which observed features support the description.
assessmentProtocols.positive: Names or locates distinct familiar areas and describes supported distinguishing characteristics, rather than only point to an isolated object.
assessmentProtocols.nearMiss: Lists two objects without identifying areas or gives characteristics unsupported by the supplied local evidence.
assessmentProtocols.transfer: Identify and describe different areas on another familiar local/school plan with its own evidence and key.
assessmentProtocols.coverageBoundary: The source requires some distinct areas and characteristics. Residential/commercial/mixed-use examples are illustrative, not a mandatory universal functional classification, mixed-use analysis or zoning-law claim. Existing map/feature knowledge and this task suffice; no new land-use topic is introduced.

assessmentProtocols.materials: Adult-prepared accurate own-community cards for a natural feature, built feature and services/jobs, including a service used by the learner. The source facts explain what each provides. Worked resources: City of Toronto drinking-water treatment/supply and the previously verified garbage/organics and public-library cards; adapt the provider to the actual community rather than assume Toronto services everywhere.
task: Identify a natural/built feature and services/occupations in the actual community and explain how people, including the learner, use them to meet needs.
Distinguish a needed benefit from merely a preferred object. Explain the link between the feature/service, what people do and the need it helps meet.
For one feature and one service, explain a reasonable consequence if it were unavailable; supply necessary factual limits, rather than demand engineering or institutional knowledge.
Use another actual feature/service to check transfer; do not assume every person uses the community in the same way.
assessmentProtocols.positive: Explains supported people–feature/service–need relationships, including own use and a plausible absence consequence.
assessmentProtocols.nearMiss: Lists places or job names without their relationship to needs, or claims all communities have the same provider/way of meeting a need.
assessmentProtocols.transfer: Another verified natural/built feature or service, retaining its actual people/benefit relationship.

sources.role: City describes obtaining LakeOntario water, treating/testing and supplying it to residents/businesses/visitors. Use only introductory service/need facts; chemical treatment calculations and drinking demonstrations are not task requirements.
Current waste-service facts, with residential recycling operator distinction retained.
Actual public-library provider/service; use its matching borrowing-resource card.

assessmentProtocols.wholeClaimBoundary: The existing needs/wants, job/service, local-feature and consequences claims remain unchanged. Source-specific integration does not require a new younger council, public-service or environmental-needs topic.

assessmentProtocols.materials: Verified familiar school/community place and relevant local care/service information, plus a simple map and ordinary drawing/planning materials. Use the actual site’s accessible disposal or care arrangements; no invented bin/provider location.
task: Choose a specific responsible action for the familiar built/natural place and state what is to be improved.
Create an ordered plan naming materials/information, where actions occur and who should do them; distinguish the learner’s part from an adult/provider responsibility.
Explain how the planned actions could enhance the actual place, using supplied facts and a plausible consequence rather than promise a measured environmental outcome.
Revise the plan when a resource/location changes and explain the revision.
assessmentProtocols.positive: A specific workable local plan with steps, relevant resources and an explained place-care benefit.
assessmentProtocols.nearMiss: Only says be good or clean up without a plan, location or explanation of the effect.
assessmentProtocols.transfer: Another familiar place or changed resource constraint.
assessmentProtocols.wholeClaimBoundary: Source requires creating/explaining a plan, not carrying out a cleanup or a classroom outcome study. Actual performance of the planning operation remains required in the task.

assessmentProtocols.materials: A familiar visited school/local place, adult-verified landmarks and suitable equal non-standard length units (such as floor-tile intervals or a repeatable classroom unit). Use the same origin when comparing distances. Provide any access/path facts needed.
task: Describe significant local places using relative position and direction, and compare which is closer/farther from the same reference point using actual route lengths or a direct model of them.

Measure a short familiar route using equal units and record the number with its unit. If comparing modelled routes directly, align them to the same origin instead of comparing only their paper positions.

Construct a simple map of the visited place with symbols and a key, and put the route’s non-standard-unit distance on that same map. Use a consistent stated unit so the symbols and distance describe the actual route together.
Use the map to describe another location/direction or distance relationship and explain a changed comparison when the reference point changes.
assessmentProtocols.positive: Uses relative location/distance/direction meaningfully and integrates symbols plus an accurately recorded non-standard route unit on one familiar-place map.
assessmentProtocols.nearMiss: Says farther without a common reference, uses unequal units/gaps, or produces an unrelated drawing and separate length result without connecting them.
assessmentProtocols.transfer: Another visited familiar place or a changed reference point while preserving consistent units and map-key meanings.
assessmentProtocols.wholeClaimBoundary: No formal numerical scale, cardinal-direction system or advanced cartographic calculation is added. Source examples do not make every representation mandatory; this task accounts for its actual symbol/non-standard-unit and relative-language requirements.

assessmentProtocols.materials: Combine the already reviewed own-school territory packet, distinct-local-area map and actual service cards with the relative-distance/symbol-unit task above. These refer to the same learner’s familiar community, not disconnected textbook exercises.
task: Describe significant local areas, natural/built features and services with accurate examples from the prepared community packet.
Identify the school’s supported traditional/treaty references using the separately reviewed attributed protocol, retaining its source/map limitations.
Use the familiar map to describe locations/directions and compare or measure distance using the same reference and unit.
Explain how the different representations and examples describe one community, retaining uncertainty where the local resources do not establish a fact.
assessmentProtocols.positive: Coherently describes actual community features/areas/services and uses basic location/distance representations; prior component protocols are part of the task, not replaced by a summary label.
assessmentProtocols.nearMiss: Names unrelated places without local evidence or succeeds in isolated components but cannot connect the map/distance to the described community.
assessmentProtocols.transfer: A second familiar community area or changed reference point with its appropriate source facts.
assessmentProtocols.wholeClaimBoundary: Full authoring judgment requires the prior reviewed territory/area/service protocols together with this integration, not this task title alone.

assessmentProtocols.materials: Adult prepares dated actual school/classroom routine accounts, relevant object/place information, an accurate familiar-place plan and actual comparable duty/action records. For a question about changing responsibilities, specify a common observation unit (for example, one expected duty in complete first-week/current-week schedules covering the same number of school days), distinguish expected assignments from observed actions, and verify record coverage. The learner chooses a non-sensitive real starting-school/new-class event and an actual learner/pupil/helper relationship. Their own voluntary account of what they thought/felt is a firsthand source; do not assign a feeling or force a positive self-description.

clauseTasks.A2.1: Formulate a question about how the real event/place/people relate to the learner’s role, relationship, duties or sense of capability/self. Refine an unrelated name/date question into one that could investigate the relationship.
clauseTasks.A2.2: Gather relevant information from the supplied dated accounts/objects and voluntary own recollection; organize it in an event/source table or timeline. Distinguish what the source says from what is inferred, and identify who/what it concerns.
clauseTasks.A2.3: Analyse the actual familiar school/classroom plan and construct a simple map with key/labels showing places significant to the event/role relationship. Use the map within the question, not as an unrelated route worksheet.
clauseTasks.A2.4: Interpret the timeline and relevant role/duty table to explain continuity/change and its relation to self-description. Use a graph/display only when the chosen question needs a count or comparison supported by actual comparable records, with the observation unit, period and coverage explicit. For changing responsibilities, compare the recorded duties under the same rule; use a meaningful labelled diagram and simple classification key for their people/place-care roles. Do not count source mentions just to make a chart, equate expected duties with completed actions, or infer confidence/identity from duty totals. A map legend alone is not a classification key.
clauseTasks.A2.5: Evaluate which dated source/clue supports the question and which is unrelated or insufficient. Draw a conclusion connecting actual role/duty/situation evidence with the learner’s own self-description, including supported continuity or uncertainty. Do not infer identity directly from an activity count. Make a tentative prediction for another transition and suggest how a clearer date, another appropriate account or better question could improve the inquiry.
clauseTasks.A2.6: Communicate the actual findings in a chosen oral/visual/written form, using role, relationship, responsibility and identity/sense-of-self vocabulary accurately. Identify a source and a limit, and explain what the representations show rather than merely display them.

assessmentProtocols.integratedTask: Complete these stages around the same actual question and self-application. The earlier fictional Ari role case rehearses concepts but does not replace the learner’s own-role investigation. Connect the event/situation, roles/relationships/duties and sense of self; change is not assumed where evidence supports continuity.
assessmentProtocols.positive: A coherent source-supported explanation answering the actual question, integrating meaningful map/data/history tools and authentic self-application with a justified conclusion, tentative prediction and improvement.
assessmentProtocols.nearMiss: A polished timeline or map disconnected from the question; a feeling label with no role/self relationship; a made-up personal event; or a claim stronger than the available evidence.
assessmentProtocols.transfer: A different non-sensitive real classroom/community transition or relationship, retaining the inquiry process while checking which facts changed.
assessmentProtocols.resourceCondition: If the adult cannot verify a local event/source or the learner does not wish to discuss an example, select another ordinary real learner role/event. Do not substitute a fictional success as certification of mandatory own-role application.

assessmentProtocols.materials: Adult prepares an actual local natural/built-feature change packet with dated earlier/current accounts or observations, an accurate local map and relevant comparable data. For a quantitative question, use actual dated observations/tallies with a common unit, defined site boundaries and consistent coverage (for example, one visible litter item within the same mapped path/planted-bed survey zones at comparable times before/after a local change). Supply an appropriate longer-term record/account as well as immediate effects; distinguish documented facts, project intentions and uncertain outcomes. LovePark remains a qualitative documentary worked example, not a source of invented numerical outcomes.

clauseTasks.B2.1: Formulate a question about people’s interaction with actual natural/built features and short- versus long-term effects. Ask what could be found from the supplied records and what another observation would need to check.
clauseTasks.B2.2: Gather/organize dated information about the actual feature change and its effects. Record source/date and separate direct observation, documentary statement and inference. Use a table and clearly defined categories rather than fabricate counts or treat a promotional intention as a measured outcome.
clauseTasks.B2.3: Analyse and construct a simple map of significant natural/built features in the inquiry with title, labels, meaningful symbols/key and suitable relative locations. Relate a mapped change to the question; do not infer a north arrow or survey scale from an unannotated photograph.
clauseTasks.B2.4: Interpret representations that materially address the question. Keep the LovePark worked case qualitative: its chronology, map/diagram and documented changes do not establish quantitative outcome trends. For the actual own-community quantitative packet, use a relevant table/bar/pictorial display only from comparable observations, with defined units, dates, site boundaries and coverage. A simple supplied location/feature classification key can separate observed items in mapped path versus planted-bed zones where this helps answer the question; explain exclusions consistently. Do not count source mentions, invent physical counts, use an irrelevant chart or confuse a map legend with a classification key.
clauseTasks.B2.5: Compare the relevance/support of records to the question and draw an appropriately limited conclusion about actual short/long-term effects. Explain whose account is represented, distinguish recorded construction/physical changes from unmeasured benefits, make a tentative prediction and suggest a comparable observation/source that would improve the inquiry. Do not infer causation from two dates alone.
clauseTasks.B2.6: Communicate supported findings in an appropriate chosen form using place/map/symbol/distance/direction/community vocabulary accurately; retain the time contrast, attribution and uncertainty.

assessmentProtocols.integratedTask: Investigate the same own-community question through the complete cycle. The LovePark packet shows an authentic documentary pathway; its facts do not automatically describe every learner’s community. Natural and built features and short/long-term effects remain visible throughout.
assessmentProtocols.positive: A coherent inquiry using actual local evidence and maps/data tools, with justified time-sensitive conclusions, an appropriate prediction/improvement and clear communication of both support and limits.
assessmentProtocols.nearMiss: A generic cleanup slogan, isolated graph/map, invented local data, treating every advertised benefit as a measured effect, or concluding that all people have one view of a change.
assessmentProtocols.transfer: Another actual local feature change with its own evidence and time scale; adapt the question and representation instead of copying a conclusion.

workedCase.authority: Waterfront Toronto, project delivery account; photographs attributed on the page to CCxA
verifiedFacts: Park construction ran July2021–June2023; park opened June2023.
The account identifies retained mature trees, new planting, paths and public-space uses.
A construction liaison committee addressed issues including noise, traffic and debris.
workedCase.sourceUse: Use a paraphrased dated event table/chronology and attributed current feature description qualitatively. The privately inspected aerial supports identifying visible pond/tree/path/grass areas; no numerical visitor/ecological outcome is derived from it. Consult the source image where permitted; no image is redistributed.
workedCase.shortLongContrast: Construction-period issues and physical change differ from the later public park and its continued planned uses. The source documents the project, not an independent long-term biodiversity/health evaluation.
workedCase.mapBoundary: The aerial is a viewpoint, not a surveyed north-up map; use its relative feature positions and the official location, and identify what orientation/scale is unverified.
workedCase.evidenceLimit: Do not invent complaint counts, visitor numbers, tree-survival rates, wildlife increases or measured wellbeing effects. For an outcome question, explicitly state what new comparable evidence would be needed.

assessmentProtocols.resourceCondition: Own-community performance uses a verified actual local packet. If dates/effects are not established, narrow the question or identify what remains unknown; do not present a synthetic rehearsal dataset as actual community evidence.

B3.1 territory/treaty knowledge and own-school verified-resource protocol; no universal parcel determination or learner-study requirement.
